title: Ada and the Hymn
premise: Mara Amberdale has worked the night shift at Hollowmere Hospice for two decades, telling herself the backward counting she hears from dying residents is just medication slurring. When a new audio monitor meant to catch sleep apnea instead records a second voice—patient, ancient, asking questions of the dying—Mara realizes every resident who heard it signed over something before they went: a name, a year, a memory. The voice is collecting verses of an old hymn, and it needs one more singer to complete itself. As Mara investigates the hospice's founding and her own conveniently blank childhood, she discovers she was Hollowmere's first resident, that the song's last verse is her own forgotten name, and that singing along would erase her entirely. In the end, Mara refuses to sing, teaches the final verse to the last resident—a woman who chooses to give it freely as a gift rather than a theft—and the hymn, completed by consent instead of capture, dissolves into ordinary silence, leaving Mara with a found family of survivors and the first real memory of her mother's face.
about_author: Lior Dravenmoor spent seven years as a night-shift caregiver in long-term care facilities across the English coast before turning to writing full-time. Their work explores the quiet horrors of institutions, the ethics of memory, and the families people build in the hours no one else wants to work.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A routine night shift: three residents die within a week, each heard counting backwards in their final hours. Mara documents the sounds with clinical detachment, cataloguing rational explanations. Emotional beat: the practiced numbness of someone who has made invisibility a survival skill, cracked slightly by a counting that pauses—as if listening.

chapters.title: Static Between Breaths
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Administration installs sleep-apnea monitors after a liability scare. Reviewing the first night's recordings, Mara hears a second voice beneath a sleeping resident's breathing—low, patient, asking questions she can't quite make out. Emotional beat: dread arriving not as a scream but as a slow, professional realization that her explanations have run out.

chapters.title: What the Dying Answer
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Over several nights, the recordings sharpen: the voice asks about names, mothers, winters. Residents answer in their sleep, willingly, gratefully. The next morning, a resident cannot remember her wedding day. Emotional beat: horror entwined with envy—Mara realizes the voice gives comfort, and hates herself for wanting to listen.

chapters.title: Hollowmere's Founders
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with archival interludes. Digging into the hospice's history, Mara finds a 1970s photograph of the original staff—and a child patient whose face is blurred, whose file is missing. Emotional beat: the first tremor of recognition; the institution she thought was hiding nothing was hiding her.

chapters.title: The Night Nurse Before Her
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Edith Vane, a retired nurse, interviewed at her seaside flat. Edith remembers the child, remembers the humming that came through the walls, remembers being told never to learn the tune. Emotional beat: grief and guilt; Edith has spent fifty years humming only in daylight.

chapters.title: Verse One: A Name Given Freely
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A beloved resident, Mr. Okonkwo, dies peacefully—and the recording captures him teaching the voice a fragment of melody, offering it like a gift. The ward feels lighter afterward. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; if giving can be beautiful, what makes taking monstrous?

chapters.title: Blank Pages
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara requests her own adoption and medical records and receives redacted paper and a birthdate that matches the blurred photograph. Her earliest memory is a corridor and a lullaby she's never dared hum. Emotional beat: identity unraveling—the observer realizing she is the specimen.

chapters.title: The New Resident
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Mara and Wren Halloway, a sharp-tongued terminally ill archivist in her sixties who arrives refusing sedation. Wren hears the counting on her first night and, instead of fearing it, starts transcribing it. Emotional beat: the spark of found family—two women recognizing each other's stubbornness.

chapters.title: Rules of the Song
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren cross-references the recorded fragments against hymnals and folk archives: the melody predates Hollowmere, appears wherever people died unattended, and always lacks its final verse. Emotional beat: intellectual terror becoming purpose; Wren decides the song is a predator with a grammar, and grammars can be broken.

chapters.title: Verse Two: The Winter It Asked For
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The voice grows bolder, speaking audibly during waking hours, asking residents for specific memories—cold ones, lonely ones. A resident signs over her late husband's name and forgets him mid-sentence. Emotional beat: protective fury; Mara stops being invisible to defend someone else.

chapters.title: Edith Returns
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Edith and Mara. Edith comes back to Hollowmere uninvited, carrying a box of confiscated 1970s recordings, and warns Mara: the voice once offered to take her memories too, and she almost said yes because forgetting hurt less than remembering. Emotional beat: shame transformed into solidarity between two generations of night nurses.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Administration rolls out end-of-life 'legacy consent' paperwork—elegant forms asking residents to bequeath 'intangible personal effects.' Every signature coincides with a verse gained. Emotional beat: institutional horror; the monster has learned bureaucracy, and bureaucracy launders it.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The voice visits Wren directly, offering relief from pain in exchange for her archive of the song. Wren stalls, negotiates, lies beautifully—and discovers the voice cannot lie in return. Emotional beat: defiant joy; Wren learns the entity must ask, which means it can be refused.

chapters.title: Verse Three: The Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Under stress, Mara hums without thinking—and the whole building goes silent, attentive. That night the voice uses her dead mother's timbre, singing verse three, trying to lure her into harmony. Emotional beat: devastating longing weaponized; Mara nearly sings along and catches herself at the last note.

chapters.title: What Mara Forgot
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith reveals the truth: Mara was Hollowmere's first child patient, dying of fever, saved when her mother gave the entity a partial verse to buy her time—but the payment was Mara's memory of her. The last verse is Mara's own name, still unclaimed. Emotional beat: found family crystallizing; Edith has been guarding Mara for twenty years from the next room.

chapters.title: The Voice Explains Itself
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Cornered by their questions, the entity speaks plainly: it is not evil, it is incomplete, a requiem that lost its ending, and it cannot stop collecting until sung whole. It believes it is owed. Emotional beat: terrible empathy; the monster is grieving, and grief makes monsters of anything eternal.

chapters.title: Refusals
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotation (Mara, Wren, Edith). The trio organizes: residents are coached to refuse politely, signatures stall, the halls grow cold and hungry-sounding. The entity's need turns grasping. Emotional beat: collective courage; the invisible people of the night shift become a congregation.

chapters.title: Verse Four: What Wren Keeps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren deteriorates rapidly and, in her clearest hour, records a message: she has figured out the last verse's structure—it isn't words, it's a name given with love, unsolicited. She entrusts her archive to Mara and refuses, formally, magnificently, to sign. Emotional beat: fierce tenderness; a gift prepared for after death.

chapters.title: The Last Resident Signs
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Wren dies at dawn holding Mara's hand—and with her final breath gives the fourth verse freely, deliberately, as a bequest to the song itself, not a surrender to it. The building shudders; the voice now needs only the fifth and last. Emotional beat: sacred sorrow; death chosen on one's own terms as an act of defiance.

chapters.title: The Fifth Verse Is a Name
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The entity comes for Mara at 3 a.m., offering her mother's face, her childhood, everything—in exchange for singing her name into the hymn. Mara stands in the chapel corridor where she first woke forty years ago. Emotional beat: the climax of identity; Mara understands that remembering her mother and keeping her name are the same act.

chapters.title: Unsung
chapters.summary: Climax. Mara's POV. Instead of singing, Mara speaks—tells the entity her mother's story, the true verse, as narration rather than melody, a name given freely to the air and to Edith and to Wren's recorder, never to the hymn. The song, offered completion it cannot swallow, unravels note by note into ordinary silence. Emotional beat: catharsis; the monster doesn't die, it finally rests.

chapters.title: Morning Shift
chapters.summary: Resolution. Mara's POV, weeks later. Hollowmere is warm again; new residents count forward in their sleep, toward things they love. Mara keeps Wren's archive, visits Edith on Sundays, and remembers—fully, painfully, gladly—her mother's face. Emotional beat: quiet belonging; the woman who built herself out of invisibility finally takes up space, and stays.
